title: The cycle (Judges 2:11–19)
hook: the people stray, suffer, cry out, and a judge rescues them, again and again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joshua at Shechem, and a choice made twice. Your line was choose this day. Did you tell someone what you decided? Today, a new book, and what happens to that choice. Day seven hundred ten.

A washing machine has a dial. Wash, rinse, spin, and round again to the start. The book of Judges has one too, and it shows it to you before the first story. Joshua is gone. His generation is gone. And the text says plainly that another generation arose after them, "which knew not the LORD." Nobody rebels in a single dramatic moment. People forget. And from that forgetting, the book sets its dial turning, and it keeps turning for chapter after chapter.
screen: `WASH, RINSE, SPIN, AND ROUND AGAIN.` → `A GENERATION WHICH KNEW NOT THE LORD.` → `THE DIAL STARTS TURNING.`

segments.voice: Chapter two lays out the whole pattern in a few verses, like a summary on the back of a book. First, the people stray: they serve the gods of the land and forsake the Lord who brought them out of Egypt. Second, they suffer: they're handed over to raiders and enemies, and they're greatly distressed. Third, they cry out: the passage calls it their groaning. Fourth, the Lord raises up a shofet, and the shofet saves them. And then the turn: when the shofet dies, they go back, the text says, and do worse than their fathers. Then the dial comes round again. Shofet is today's word. It's usually translated judge, and the book is called Shoftim, Judges. But in this book a shofet is mostly not someone in a courtroom. The text says the Lord raised up judges who delivered them out of the hand of those who plundered them. A shofet is a rescuer, raised up in a crisis, who leads while they live. Two details in the passage are worth slowing down for. The first: why does God send a rescuer? The text doesn't say the people repented. It says the Lord was moved by their groaning, because of those who oppressed and crushed them. The help comes in answer to pain, before anyone has changed. The second: the cycle isn't a perfect circle. When each judge dies, the text says, the people turn back and act more corruptly than their fathers. Each time round, a little lower. That's what keeps the book from being simply repetitive. It's a pattern you can watch, and name, and, once you see it, start to recognize in other places.
screen: `STRAY, SUFFER, CRY OUT.` · `A SHOFET IS RAISED UP AND SAVES.` · `MOVED BY THEIR GROANING.` · then, large: `EACH TIME ROUND, A LITTLE LOWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one cycle you repeat. Let one pattern in your own life come to mind, small is fine: the late night that leads to the bad morning, the argument that always starts the same way, the promise to yourself that fades by the weekend. Walk it through its stages, the way chapter two does. Where does it start? What's the forgetting? Where does it hurt? What do you do when it does? Don't try to fix it now. Just see the dial. The bell holds the time.
Shofet. Judge, in the book of Judges: a rescuer the Lord raises up when the people cry out, who leads them while they live. Today's word.
Your line: the cycle repeats. Today, when your pattern starts its first turn, name the stage you're in, out loud or in your head. Day seven hundred ten.

howItsDone: Jews read Judges, Shoftim, among the Former Prophets, right after Joshua; its chapter two sets out the pattern of straying, oppression, crying out and rescue that the later stories follow.

original.note: Hebrew: judge. the book of Judges is called Shoftim, judges.

trapdoor: what you thought: judges in robes, deciding cases.
what it means: rescuers raised up when the people cry out, who lead while they live.
what a scholar hears: chapter two tells the plot before the stories begin, so each later judge is read against this pattern.

notes: Auditor: 2:11–19 never uses 'cry out' (2:18 has 'groanings'), so the teach now says so; 'each time round, the text says, it goes a little lower' tied to what 2:19 actually says.
Judges 2:10 is quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 may read 'that knew not the LORD'. Confirm and switch the citation if preferred.
The four stages are this script's teaching summary of 2:11–19, not the text's own numbering.
'Moved by their groaning' paraphrases 2:18 ('it repented the LORD because of their groanings', KJV); translations differ on the verb.
Deborah, who judges cases (4:5), is the exception that comes in two days; not mentioned here.
